title: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
summary: How a PC decides what code to trust before the OS starts: UEFI, SPI flash locks, Secure Boot keys and revocation, TPM measured boot and attestation, hardware roots of trust, and the bootkits that broke each.
outcomes: Explain the UEFI boot phases and where firmware implants, bootkits and their defences sit in the chain
Apply the UEFI db and dbx rules to decide whether an image boots, and explain hash versus certificate revocation
Explain why BlackLotus worked after a patch and what the 2023 to 2026 Microsoft certificate rollover changes
Compute PCR extends and replay a TCG event log to detect an edited log
Check a remote attestation quote correctly, including the nonce, and state what it cannot prove
Compare Intel Boot Guard, AMD PSB and Apple silicon boot by what each verifies and what it misses
Spot vulnerable firmware logic (flash locks, parsers, loaders, update rollback) and describe the fix
Build a firmware defence checklist and name the signal each layer produces

lessons.title: Below the operating system: why boot code is the deepest foothold

blocks.md:
Plain idea: every security control you met in the prereq courses (rings, the reference monitor, Secure Boot for the kernel, ASLR, CFI) is enforced by code that has to be loaded by something earlier. Whoever controls that earlier code decides what the later code sees.

A tiny example. You reinstall Windows on an infected laptop and swap in a brand-new disk. The malware comes back on the first boot. That is what ESET, a security software company, found in 2018 with **LoJax**: a malicious module written into the laptop's firmware chip, which re-installed its Windows agent at every boot and so survived both an OS reinstall and a disk replacement ([ESET](https://www.welivesecurity.com/2018/09/27/lojax-first-uefi-rootkit-found-wild-courtesy-sednit-group/)).

Terms used all course:

- **Firmware**: software stored on a chip on the board rather than on the disk; it runs first when the machine powers on.
- **BIOS** (Basic Input/Output System): the original PC firmware. **UEFI** (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) is the specification that replaced it on modern PCs; it defines how firmware starts the machine and hands over to an operating system.
- **SPI flash** (SPI: Serial Peripheral Interface, the simple serial bus it sits on): the small chip soldered to the motherboard that stores the firmware.
- **Bootloader**: the program firmware starts, which in turn loads the OS kernel.
- **Bootkit**: in Microsoft's words, a malicious program designed to load as early as possible in the boot sequence to control the operating system start ([KB5025885](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/topic/kb5025885-how-to-manage-the-windows-boot-manager-revocations-for-secure-boot-changes-associated-with-cve-2023-24932-41a975df-beb2-40c1-99a3-b3ff139f832d)). A **firmware implant** (or UEFI rootkit) goes one step lower and lives in the SPI flash itself.

blocks.title: Where boot-level malware can live, and what it survives

scenes.caption: Each layer starts the next one. Code at a lower layer runs first and can change or hide anything above it.
An OS reinstall rewrites the disk: apps, kernel and normally the boot partition. Malware in the kernel or apps is gone.
A bootkit on the ESP survives if the reinstall keeps that partition, and it starts before every kernel defence.
A new disk removes the ESP too. Only the motherboard's SPI flash remains, which is where LoJax lived.
Code burned into ROM or fuses cannot be changed by malware at all. That is why hardware roots of trust (lesson 12) anchor the chain there.

blocks.md:
Why defenders care about each layer:

- **Persistence.** The lower the layer, the more cleanups it survives. ESET notes that removing a firmware implant means reflashing the SPI chip with a clean image or replacing the motherboard.
- **Privilege.** Boot code runs before the kernel's protections exist, so it can switch them off. BlackLotus (lesson 7) disabled BitLocker (Windows full-disk encryption), HVCI (Hypervisor-protected Code Integrity, also called memory integrity: the hypervisor lets only signed kernel code become executable) and Microsoft Defender.
- **Visibility.** Endpoint tools run inside the OS. CERT/CC (the CERT Coordination Center at Carnegie Mellon University, which coordinates vulnerability disclosure) notes that UEFI firmware is largely invisible to most EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) products ([VU#455367](https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/455367)).

The rest of this course follows one question layer by layer: what is checked, by whom, with which key, and what happens when that check is missing, buggy or trusts the wrong thing.

A check can only be as trustworthy as the code that performs it. Boot security is a chain: each stage verifies or measures the next, and the chain is only as strong as its first link and its weakest check.
Misconception: "I reinstalled the OS, so the machine is clean." A reinstall cleans the disk. It does not touch the SPI flash, and it may not touch every file on the boot partition.

blocks.question: An incident responder wipes a server's disks and reinstalls the OS, but the same backdoor reappears within minutes of the first boot. Which location best explains this?
options: A scheduled task in the new OS image
A browser extension synced from the cloud
An implant in the motherboard's SPI flash that rewrites the backdoor at boot
A malicious kernel module on the old disk
blocks.explain: Only the SPI flash survives a disk wipe and reinstall. A firmware implant such as LoJax (lesson 15) drops its payload into the fresh OS on every boot. The old disk is gone, and a fresh image has no scheduled task unless something wrote one.

blocks.question: Why does boot-level malware run with an advantage over EDR software?
options: It runs before the OS and its security agents start, so it can disable or hide from them
EDR is not allowed to read files
Firmware runs faster than the OS
EDR only scans network traffic
blocks.explain: Boot code runs first. It can change what the kernel loads and turn protections off before any agent starts, and the firmware itself is largely invisible to tools running in the OS.

lessons.title: From power-on to the OS loader: UEFI phases, variables and the ESP

blocks.md:
Plain idea: UEFI firmware is not one program but a sequence of phases, each with more of the machine working than the last. You need the names because advisories say things like "memory corruption in the DXE phase".

The phases come from the **PI** (Platform Initialization) specification, the companion to UEFI published by the UEFI Forum ([PI spec](https://uefi.org/specs/PI/1.8/V1_Security_SEC_Phase_Information.html)). Here is the conceptual sequence, simplified:

scenes.caption: SEC (Security) runs first after reset, with no RAM yet: it uses CPU cache as temporary memory. The PI spec calls SEC the root of trust of the system.
PEI (Pre-EFI Initialization) brings up permanent memory and describes it in Hand-Off Blocks for the next phase.
DXE (Driver Execution Environment) loads most firmware drivers: storage, network, graphics, and image parsers for the boot logo. Most firmware bugs in this course live here.
BDS (Boot Device Selection) reads the boot order variables and starts a boot application from disk, such as Windows Boot Manager or shim.
The OS loader still has UEFI boot services available until it calls ExitBootServices(). After that, only runtime services remain and the OS owns the machine.

blocks.md:
Three pieces of UEFI state matter for security:

- **UEFI variables**: small named values kept in non-volatile storage (NVRAM, usually a region of the same SPI flash). The boot order, the Secure Boot keys and settings live here. Some variables are **boot-services-only**: readable and writable only before `ExitBootServices()`, so the running OS cannot touch them.
- **The ESP** (EFI System Partition): a FAT-formatted disk partition the firmware reads boot applications from, for example `EFI/Microsoft/Boot/bootmgfw.efi`. CERT/CC describes it as the storage place for UEFI boot loaders, applications, drivers and settings, protected from unprivileged access ([VU#811862](https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/811862)). An administrator can write to it.
- **Boot services vs runtime services**: boot services (loading images, reading disks) end at `ExitBootServices()`; runtime services such as `GetVariable()` and `SetVariable()` stay callable by the OS.

blocks.prompt: A bootkit needs to change a boot-services-only variable, such as the list of extra keys shim trusts. From the running OS it cannot. What would it need instead?
blocks.reveal: Code execution **before** `ExitBootServices()`, inside the boot path. That is exactly why BlackLotus needed a Secure Boot bypass: ESET explains that exploiting CVE-2022-21894 gave it code execution while boot services were still available, which let it write the boot-services-only `MokList` variable (shim's list of Machine Owner Keys, lesson 5). Without such a bug, changing it needs a person at the keyboard during boot.

blocks.md: When you read an advisory, map the bug to a phase. SEC or PEI bugs run before memory is even set up; DXE bugs run with all drivers but before the OS; bugs in a boot application run after BDS. Then ask what input reaches the bug: anything an OS administrator can write (ESP files, NVRAM variables, update capsules) makes it reachable from a compromised OS.

blocks.question: Which statement about `ExitBootServices()` is correct?
options: It is called by the firmware before DXE starts
It erases the ESP
It turns Secure Boot off
After it, boot-services-only variables are no longer writable by the OS
blocks.explain: The OS loader calls ExitBootServices() to take ownership of the machine. From then on only runtime services remain, and variables marked boot-services-only can no longer be read or written.

blocks.question: An administrator-level attacker on a running Windows machine wants to plant a file that firmware will process at the next boot. Which location is within reach without any firmware bug?
options: The boot ROM
The CPU fuses
The EFI System Partition
SMRAM
blocks.explain: The ESP is an ordinary partition an administrator can write. That is why bootkits and the LogoFAIL logo files live there. The boot ROM and fuses are read-only, and SMRAM is locked away from the OS (next lesson).

lessons.title: SPI flash, SMM and the write lock LoJax walked through

blocks.md:
Plain idea: the firmware lives in a flash chip the OS can talk to, because firmware must be updatable. So the platform needs a lock that lets the *real* update path write the chip and stops everything else. On many Intel PCs that lock relied on **SMM**.

**SMM** (System Management Mode) is a special x86 CPU mode, more privileged in practice than the kernel. The CPU enters it on an **SMI** (System Management Interrupt) and runs firmware handlers from **SMRAM**, memory the OS cannot read or write. The PI spec generalises this as **MM** (Management Mode): an isolated execution environment, implemented by SMM on x86 and by TrustZone (Arm's hardware-isolated secure world) on Arm, whose handlers stay resident while the OS runs ([PI spec, MM overview](https://uefi.org/specs/PI/1.8/V4_Overview.html)). Because SMM code outlives boot and is reachable from the OS through SMIs, a bug in an SMI handler is a firmware-level bug at runtime.

On Intel chipsets of that era, three bits in the **BIOS_CNTL** register controlled writes to the BIOS region of the flash ([ESET LoJax white paper](https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/ESET-LoJax.pdf)):

- **BIOSWE** (BIOS Write Enable): must be 1 to write the BIOS region.
- **BLE** (BIOS Lock Enable): when set, any attempt to set BIOSWE to 1 raises an SMI, and the firmware's SMI handler is supposed to put BIOSWE back to 0 if the write is not authorised.
- **SMM_BWP** (SMM BIOS Write Protect): when set, the BIOS region is writable only if all cores are in SMM *and* BIOSWE is 1.

The flaw: with BLE, the bit really does become 1 first, and only then does the SMI handler clear it. CERT/CC (note VU#766164, credited to Corey Kallenberg and Rafal Wojtczuk) describes the race: writes can land between the moment BIOSWE is set and the moment the SMI clears it ([VU#766164](https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/766164)). And if a firmware never implemented the handler, BLE did nothing at all.

blocks.code:
# Toy model of the BIOS_CNTL write lock. Nothing here touches hardware.
# W = a flash write landed in that tick, . = it was refused.
SMI_DELAY = 2   # ticks until the SMI handler clears BIOSWE (real: microseconds)

def run(ble, smm_bwp, keep_setting, ticks=8):
    bioswe, smi_due, out = 0, None, ""
    for t in range(ticks):
        if keep_setting or t == 0:
            bioswe = 1                       # OS asks for write enable
            if ble and smi_due is None:
                smi_due = t + SMI_DELAY      # BLE: an SMI is raised
        in_smm = False                       # OS code never runs in SMM
        ok = bioswe and (not smm_bwp or in_smm)
        out += "W" if ok else "."
        if smi_due == t:
            bioswe, smi_due = 0, None        # handler clears the bit
    return out

print("no BLE, one request    :", run(0, 0, False))
print("BLE, one request       :", run(1, 0, False))
print("BLE, request every tick:", run(1, 0, True))
print("BLE + SMM_BWP, racing  :", run(1, 1, True))
blocks.caption: Toy model, runnable anywhere: no register is read or written. A tick stands for a short time step; on real hardware the window is tiny, which is why the attack used two threads racing in a loop.

blocks.code:
no BLE, one request    : WWWWWWWW
BLE, one request       : WWW.....
BLE, request every tick: WWWWWWWW
BLE + SMM_BWP, racing  : ........
blocks.caption: Real output. With BLE alone, one request still leaves a window (the W's before the handler runs), and a requester that keeps setting the bit keeps the window open. SMM_BWP closes it because OS code is never in SMM.

blocks.title: BLE alone vs BLE plus SMM_BWP (toy model)

scenes.caption: Before anything happens: BIOSWE is 0 and no write lands.
BLE, one request at tick 0: BIOSWE goes to 1 at once, the SMI handler clears it at tick 2. Writes in ticks 0 to 2 land: the race window.
BLE, a thread re-sets BIOSWE every tick: the handler keeps losing the race and every write lands. This is the bypass in VU#766164.
BLE plus SMM_BWP: BIOSWE can still be set, but the chipset refuses writes unless every core is in SMM. OS code never is, so nothing lands.

blocks.md:
**How LoJax used this.** ESET found three tools next to the LoJax agent, all driving **RwDrv.sys**, the kernel driver of the free RWEverything utility, which is validly signed because it belongs to legitimate software. One tool dumped platform information, one read the SPI flash to a file, one added a malicious DXE driver to that image and wrote it back. The writer only succeeded where the firmware left these locks weak: no BLE, or BLE without SMM_BWP (where it used the race). On a platform with SMM_BWP set it failed. ESET concluded the victim's firmware either did not configure these protections or the chipset predated Intel's PCH (Platform Controller Hub) family, introduced around 2008 according to ESET, which added SMM_BWP.

Intel's mitigation guidance quoted by CERT/CC: set SMM_BWP together with BLE and clear BIOSWE. ESET also lists **PRx** (Protected Range registers) among the SPI flash defences, another protection the firmware has to set.
A lock is only real if the firmware turns it on and locks it before running anything untrusted. Every one of these bits defaults to off; the firmware must configure them on every boot.

**Defender view.**

- *Prevent*: keep firmware updated; buy platforms whose firmware sets SMM_BWP, BLE and the protected ranges; prefer a hardware root of trust that verifies the firmware at every boot (lesson 12).
- *Detect*: tools read these bits without writing anything. **fwupd** (the Linux firmware update daemon) has a Host Security ID report whose checks include `org.fwupd.hsi.Spi.Bioswe`, `Spi.Ble` and `Spi.SmmBwp`; a failure on any of them means the firmware can be written from user space by root ([fwupd HSI spec](https://fwupd.github.io/libfwupdplugin/hsi.html)). Intel's open-source **CHIPSEC** framework, which ESET recommends, performs similar checks. On the OS side, the load of a known flash-access driver such as RwDrv.sys is itself a signal.
- *Respond*: compare a dump of the flash with the vendor's image; recovery means reflashing a known-good image or replacing the board.

blocks.question: A platform sets BLE but not SMM_BWP, and its SMI handler correctly clears BIOSWE. Why is the BIOS region still at risk?
options: BLE only applies after the OS boots
SMI handlers cannot run on multi-core CPUs
BLE makes the flash read-only, so no risk
BIOSWE becomes 1 before the handler clears it, so a racing writer can land writes in that window
blocks.explain: BLE reacts after the fact: setting BIOSWE takes effect, an SMI fires, and the handler resets it. A second thread writing in a loop can win the race. SMM_BWP removes the window by requiring SMM for every write.

blocks.question: Why was RwDrv.sys useful to the LoJax operators?
options: It is a validly signed driver that gives low-level hardware access, so Windows loads it
It exploited a Windows kernel bug
It disables Secure Boot
It encrypts the SPI flash
blocks.explain: The driver belongs to a legitimate utility and carries a valid signature, so the kernel loads it. Its job is to read and write hardware registers, which is exactly the access a flash writer needs.

lessons.title: Secure Boot keys: PK, KEK, db and dbx

blocks.md:
Plain idea: UEFI Secure Boot is an allow list with a deny list, protected by a small hierarchy of keys held by the device maker (the OEM, original equipment manufacturer) and Microsoft, that decides who may edit the lists. The prereq course showed the chain firmware, shim, GRUB, kernel; this lesson is about the keys and lists inside the firmware that start it.

All four objects are UEFI variables defined in the UEFI specification, chapter 32 ([UEFI 2.10](https://uefi.org/specs/UEFI/2.10/32_Secure_Boot_and_Driver_Signing.html)):

- **PK** (Platform Key): establishes trust between the platform owner and the firmware. Exactly one entry. Usually the device maker's key. Whoever holds PK's private half can replace PK and enrol KEKs.
- **KEK** (Key Exchange Key; Microsoft also calls it Key Enrollment Key): establishes trust between operating systems and the firmware. Holders of a KEK private key may update db and dbx. PCs that ship Windows carry a Microsoft KEK plus OEM KEKs ([Microsoft KB5062710](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/servicing/os/secure-boot/2025/06/windows-secure-boot-certificate-expiration-and-ca-updates)).
- **db** (the authorized signature database): certificates and hashes whose code may run.
- **dbx** (the forbidden signature database): certificates and hashes that must never run, even if db would allow them.

Two more you will meet: **dbt** (timestamp authorities) and **dbr** (recovery). The spec's rule for writing db, dbx, dbt and dbr: in **user mode** the update must be signed by a KEK or the PK; in **setup mode** (no PK enrolled) they can be written without a signature check.

scenes.caption: The PK sits at the top. Its private half authorises changes to the PK itself and to the KEK list.
KEK holders, typically Microsoft and the OEM, sign updates to db and dbx. This is how Windows Update can push a new dbx.
At boot the firmware checks each boot application against db and dbx. dbx wins: a match there blocks the image even if db allows it.
If an attacker holds the PK private key (PKfail, lesson 14), they can enrol their own KEK and rewrite both lists. The whole hierarchy falls with the top key.

blocks.md:
**Modes.** With no PK enrolled the platform is in setup mode (`SetupMode` = 1). Enrolling a PK switches it to user mode, where authenticated writes are required. UEFI 2.5 added **audit mode** (log what would fail, without blocking, for provisioning) and **deployed mode** (user mode with the mode variables made read-only).

**Defaults.** The spec lets the vendor ship `PKDefault`, `KEKDefault`, `dbDefault` and `dbxDefault`. The "restore factory keys" option in a setup menu puts these back. Microsoft's KB5025885 warns that a device whose Secure Boot settings are reset to defaults after the BlackLotus mitigations were applied will not boot; Microsoft ships a recovery application that re-adds the Windows UEFI CA 2023 certificate to db.

**Your own keys.** An organisation can replace the defaults with its own PK, KEK and db, so that only code it signs will boot. Cloudflare describes doing this on its servers, making itself the root of trust for UEFI ([Cloudflare](https://blog.cloudflare.com/anchoring-trust-a-hardware-secure-boot-story/)).

Misconception: "Secure Boot means the firmware is trusted." Secure Boot checks what the firmware *loads*. ESET's correction to the LoJax paper says it plainly: Secure Boot is designed against components from outside the SPI flash and would not have stopped an implant inside it.

blocks.question: An attacker obtains the private key of one KEK enrolled on a fleet of laptops, but not the PK. What can they do?
options: Nothing, only the PK matters
Replace the PK
Sign db and dbx updates, for example adding their own certificate to db
Read the TPM's private keys
blocks.explain: Per the UEFI spec, db and dbx updates must be signed by a KEK or the PK. A KEK holder can therefore add an allowed certificate. Replacing the PK needs the PK private key.

blocks.question: A laptop has no PK enrolled. What does the UEFI spec say about writing db?
options: It is impossible
It can be written without a signature check, because the platform is in setup mode
It needs Microsoft's signature
Only the TPM can write it
blocks.explain: With no PK the platform is in setup mode, and the signature databases can be written without signature validation. That is why a missing PK is a finding in its own right.

lessons.title: How firmware decides to run an image: db, dbx and the chain

blocks.md:
Plain idea: before the firmware starts a driver, an option ROM (firmware carried on a plug-in card such as a graphics card) or a boot application, it asks two questions. Is this image allowed by db? Is it forbidden by dbx? It runs only if the first answer is yes and the second is no. Microsoft's Secure Boot overview (KB5062710) says the same: Secure Boot authenticates firmware modules, including UEFI drivers such as option ROMs, boot loaders and applications, before execution.

The UEFI spec makes "forbidden" precise. Verification must fail if dbx contains ([UEFI 2.10, 32.6.3.3](https://uefi.org/specs/UEFI/2.10/32_Secure_Boot_and_Driver_Signing.html)):

1. the SHA-256 hash of the image itself, or
2. the hash of any certificate in the signing chain (`EFI_CERT_X509_SHA256` and friends), or
3. any certificate in the signing chain itself (`EFI_CERT_X509_GUID`).

Allowed means db holds either the image's hash or a certificate that verifies one of the image's signatures. A match can occur at any level of the chain: trusting a CA in db trusts every image that CA ever signed.

blocks.title: Tracing the check for one image

scenes.caption: Input: an older boot manager signed by a leaf certificate issued by the CA 'Win Prod PCA 2011'. db trusts that CA. dbx holds only an unrelated hash.
The image hash is computed and is not in dbx.
Neither certificate in the chain is in dbx either.
The hash is not in db, but the CA is: the image is allowed by certificate. Every image that CA signed passes this way.
Now Microsoft adds the PCA 2011 certificate itself to dbx. The chain loop finds it and the image is rejected, along with every other image under that CA.

blocks.caption: Toy verifier with made-up certificate names; runnable with Python 3 and no extra packages. Signature maths is assumed done; only the db and dbx policy is modelled.

blocks.code:
-- hash in dbx
bootmgr 2019: bad=True  good=False
bootmgr 2022: bad=True  good=True
bootmgr 2024: bad=True  good=True
-- CA in dbx
bootmgr 2019: bad=True  good=False
bootmgr 2022: bad=True  good=False
bootmgr 2024: bad=True  good=True
blocks.caption: Real output. verify_bad trusts anything with a db certificate in its chain and ignores dbx, so revocation does nothing. verify_good applies the spec rule: a revoked hash blocks one binary, a revoked CA blocks every binary it signed.

blocks.md: Revoking by hash blocks one exact file. Revoking a certificate blocks everything it ever signed, including good files. That trade-off drives the whole of lessons 6 to 8.

**Where shim fits.** Recall from the prereq course: Linux distributions boot through **shim**, a small loader Microsoft signs with its third-party UEFI CA, which then checks GRUB and the kernel against the distribution's key and the **MOK** list (Machine Owner Keys, extra keys enrolled by the machine's owner). ESET's BlackLotus write-up explains that MOK entries live in a boot-services-only variable, `MokList`, so changing them normally needs physical presence during boot.

**A wide circle of trust.** Microsoft points out that trusting its third-party UEFI CA in db trusts the boot loaders of every Linux distribution and many tools, so a bug in any of them exposes the machine; Secured-core PCs therefore ship with that CA not trusted by default ([Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/operating-system-security/system-security/secure-the-windows-10-boot-process)). Before removing it, check option ROMs: graphics and network cards are often signed by that same CA, so removing it can stop them at boot (lesson 8 shows the 2023 split that separates the two).

blocks.prompt: dbx holds the hash of a vulnerable boot manager. The vendor rebuilds the *same vulnerable code* with a one-byte change in a resource and signs it with the same certificate. Does the old dbx entry stop the new file?
blocks.reveal: No. A hash entry matches one exact file, so any rebuild, even one byte different, has a new hash and passes. That is why hash revocation is a losing game against a bug present in many builds, and why Microsoft eventually revoked the signing certificate instead (lesson 8).

blocks.question: db trusts the CA 'Contoso Boot CA'. dbx contains the certificate of one leaf that CA issued. An image is signed by a *different* leaf from the same CA. What happens?
options: Allowed: the CA is in db and nothing in this image's chain is in dbx
Rejected, because the CA is linked to a revoked leaf
Rejected, because dbx entries apply to all images
Allowed only if its hash is in db
blocks.explain: dbx is checked against the hash and the certificates in this image's own chain. The revoked leaf is not in it, and the CA in db verifies it, so it runs.

blocks.question: Which change to verify_bad fixes it correctly?
options: Check dbx for the image hash only
Check db twice
Check dbx for the image hash and for every certificate in the chain before consulting db
Skip images signed by a CA
blocks.explain: Checking only the hash misses certificate revocations such as the PCA 2011 entry. The spec requires refusing on any dbx match for the hash or any chain certificate, then requiring a db match.

lessons.title: Revocation is hard: dbx space, SBAT and secure version numbers

blocks.md:
Plain idea: when a signed boot component turns out to be vulnerable, patching it is not enough, because an attacker can carry the *old* signed copy to the machine and boot that. The old copy must be distrusted. UEFI gives two tools, both blunt: put its hash in dbx, or put its signing certificate in dbx.

The shim developers' SBAT design document quantifies the pain ([shim SBAT.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rhboot/shim/main/SBAT.md)). After **BootHole** (CVE-2020-10713, a GRUB bug from 2020), 3 certificates and 150 image hashes went into dbx on x64. That one event used about 10 kB of the roughly 32 kB of revocation storage typically available, and because of how UEFI merges lists the resulting dbx approached 15 kB, nearly half the space. Revoking whole certificates is not practical either: the Microsoft CAs sign too much, including option ROMs.

blocks.title: dbx storage after one revocation event (from the SBAT document)

scenes.caption: Firmware typically reserves about 32 kB for dbx. Every revoked hash costs space that never comes back.
One event, BootHole, added 3 certificates and 150 hashes: about 10 kB.
Merged with earlier revocations, dbx reached almost 15 kB, close to half the space. A few more events like this and there is no room left.

blocks.md:
Two ideas replace "list every bad file" with "state the minimum acceptable version":

- **SBAT** (Secure Boot Advanced Targeting) adds signed metadata to each boot component: vendor, product, component and a **security generation** number. A revocation then raises the minimum generation for a component in one small policy entry, instead of adding a hash for every vulnerable build. The minimum generations live in a UEFI variable named `SbatLevel`; components whose generation is below it are refused.
- **SVN** (Secure Version Number) for Windows Boot Manager. Microsoft's KB5025885 describes a self-revocation feature: the boot manager compares the SVN stored in firmware (as an entry in dbx) with the SVN built into itself and **refuses to run if its own is lower**. When a serious boot manager bug is fixed, Microsoft raises both numbers in the same update, so older signed boot managers stop themselves.

Both are **anti-rollback**: an authentic but older, vulnerable component is rejected because it is older, not because it is unsigned.

blocks.code:
firmware_svn = 5                  # floor stored in a firmware variable

def boot_manager_start(my_svn):   # the self-check runs inside the boot manager
    if my_svn < firmware_svn:
        return f"SVN {my_svn} < floor {firmware_svn}: refuse to run"
    return f"SVN {my_svn}: continue boot"

for svn in (3, 4, 5, 6):
    print(boot_manager_start(svn))
blocks.caption: Toy model of the boot manager's SVN self-check, as described in KB5025885. The floor only ever goes up.

blocks.code:
SVN 3 < floor 5: refuse to run
SVN 4 < floor 5: refuse to run
SVN 5: continue boot
SVN 6: continue boot
blocks.caption: Real output. Signed boot managers with SVN 3 and 4 are still validly signed, but they refuse to run once the firmware floor is 5.

blocks.md: Every anti-rollback step also breaks old *legitimate* media. KB5025885 warns that enabling the PCA 2011 revocation on a device with the April 2026 or later updates sets SVN 5.0 in firmware, which invalidates older external boot media. Rebuild recovery media before you raise the floor.

**Why vendors move slowly.** ESET's BlackLotus analysis puts it bluntly: revoking widely used Windows UEFI binaries can make thousands of outdated systems, recovery images or backups unbootable, so revocation often takes too long. That gap, between "patched" and "revoked", is exactly what BlackLotus lived in.

**Defender view.** Track three numbers per device class: the dbx version, whether the new CA certificates are in db, and the SVN floor. Inventory recovery USBs, PXE (Preboot Execution Environment, network boot) images and VM templates before raising any of them.

blocks.question: A boot component has had 40 vulnerable builds signed over five years by a CA that also signs thousands of good images. Which revocation approach scales best?
options: Add 40 hashes to dbx
Add the CA certificate to dbx
Do nothing; patched builds are enough
Raise a security generation or SVN so every build below the fixed one is rejected
blocks.explain: Hashes cost dbx space per build and miss rebuilds. Revoking the CA breaks thousands of good images. A generation or version floor rejects all older builds with one small update.

blocks.question: Why is installing the patched boot manager, without any revocation, not enough?
options: An attacker with admin rights can place the old, still-trusted, vulnerable binary on the ESP and boot it
Patched binaries are unsigned
Firmware ignores the ESP
dbx is read-only
blocks.explain: Secure Boot asks only whether a binary is trusted, not whether it is the newest. Until the old one is distrusted by hash, certificate or version, it still boots.

lessons.title: Case: Baton Drop and BlackLotus, a signed door left open

blocks.md:
Plain idea: a bug in a *signed* Windows boot component was fixed in January 2022, but the old signed copies were still trusted by every PC's db and absent from dbx. A year later, malware simply brought the old copies along.

**The bug.** CVE-2022-21894, nicknamed **Baton Drop**, is listed by NVD as a "Secure Boot Security Feature Bypass Vulnerability" ([NVD](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2022-21894)). ESET's summary of the public write-up: affected Windows boot applications could be told, through a boot configuration option, to remove the serialized Secure Boot policy from memory *before* the application loaded it. With the policy gone, options the policy normally forbids, such as test signing or disabled integrity checks, were accepted. The pattern is **fail open**: missing policy was treated as no policy.

**The malware.** On 1 March 2023 Martin Smolár of ESET published the first public analysis of **BlackLotus**, a UEFI bootkit sold on hacking forums for USD 5,000 since at least October 2022 ([ESET](https://www.welivesecurity.com/2023/03/01/blacklotus-uefi-bootkit-myth-confirmed/)). It ran on fully updated Windows 11 with Secure Boot on.

blocks.caption: Toy model of the fail-open pattern, with made-up names. It is not Windows code, uses no real boot option, and only shows why reading the policy first and refusing when it is missing is the safe design.

blocks.code:
bad : ['allow_unsigned']
good: []
blocks.caption: Real output. The vulnerable version loses the policy and then allows unsigned code; the fixed version reads the policy before honouring any option and refuses to boot without it.

blocks.title: BlackLotus persistence, at the level of ESET's write-up

scenes.caption: Step 0: the installer already has administrator rights. It turns off HVCI and suspends BitLocker so the boot changes will not trigger a recovery screen.
It writes files to the ESP: legitimate but vulnerable Microsoft-signed boot binaries, a Microsoft-signed shim, the self-signed bootkit and a crafted boot configuration.
Reboot. Firmware checks the old boot manager: its CA is in db and nothing about it is in dbx, so it runs. Secure Boot is working as configured.
Baton Drop removes the Secure Boot policy, so attacker code runs before ExitBootServices and writes its own key into the boot-only MokList variable.
Every later boot: firmware runs the genuine Microsoft-signed shim, shim trusts the MOK, and the self-signed bootkit loads. No exploit is needed any more.

blocks.md:
What the bootkit then did, per ESET: deployed a kernel driver that protects its files on the ESP from removal, and an HTTP downloader running inside `winlogon.exe` (the Windows logon process) that fetched further payloads. Microsoft's KB5025885 stresses the precondition: the attacker must already have administrative rights or physical access. BlackLotus is a persistence and stealth tool, not an initial access tool.

**Why the January 2022 patch did not help.** Patching replaced the boot manager on the disk, but db still trusted the old one and dbx did not list it. ESET noted the advertisement's own claim: adding the vulnerable binaries to dbx was impractical because the bug affected hundreds of boot loaders still in use. Microsoft tracks the Secure Boot bypass used by BlackLotus as [CVE-2023-24932](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-24932) and, as the next lesson shows, ended up distrusting the whole signing CA.

**Detection** (Microsoft's investigation guidance, [Microsoft Security blog](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2023/04/11/guidance-for-investigating-attacks-using-cve-2022-21894-the-blacklotus-campaign/), April 2023):

- Recently modified or locked boot files on the ESP (`bootmgfw.efi`, `grubx64.efi`, `winload.efi` under `EFI\Microsoft\Boot`) and a leftover `system32` staging folder at the ESP root.
- `HypervisorEnforcedCodeIntegrity` registry value `Enabled` set to 0.
- Defender operational log entries saying protection stopped, and System event 7023 for the Defender service.
- Outbound port 80 connections from `winlogon.exe`.
- Measured boot logs in `C:\Windows\Logs\MeasuredBoot`: diffing two boots shows new `EV_EFI_Boot_Services_Application` entries for `grubx64.efi` and `winload.efi`.

**Response** (ESET): reinstall, and remove the attacker's MOK with `mokutil` (the Linux tool for MOK changes), which needs someone physically at the machine during boot. Revoking the old binaries afterwards does not remove a MOK-based persistence that is already in place.
"Fixed" and "no longer trusted" are different states. Until the vulnerable signed binary is revoked or rolled past, the fix protects only machines whose attacker politely uses the new file.

blocks.question: Why did BlackLotus carry its own copies of old Microsoft boot binaries instead of using the ones on the victim's disk?
options: The victim's binaries were encrypted
The victim's binaries were patched; the old ones were still trusted by db and not in dbx, and still had the bug
Old binaries are smaller
Firmware only runs binaries downloaded from Microsoft
blocks.explain: January 2022 updates replaced the vulnerable boot manager on patched machines, but the vulnerable signed copies remained valid for Secure Boot. Bringing them along recreated the bug on demand.

blocks.question: A responder finds the attacker's key in MokList. They apply the latest dbx, which now revokes the vulnerable Windows binaries. Is the machine clean after a reboot?
options: Yes, dbx blocks the bootkit
Yes, because MokList is erased by dbx updates
No, because dbx updates disable Secure Boot
No: shim is still trusted and still trusts the MOK, so the self-signed bootkit keeps loading
blocks.explain: ESET notes that revocation after persistence is set leaves the bootkit working, because the chain now runs through a legitimately signed shim and the attacker's MOK. The MOK must be removed (with physical presence) and the system reinstalled.

blocks.md:
Plain idea: to finally kill every old vulnerable boot manager, Microsoft decided to stop trusting the certificate that signed them all, **Microsoft Windows Production PCA 2011**, and to sign new boot managers with a new one, **Windows UEFI CA 2023**. At the same time, the original 2011 certificates were reaching their expiry dates in 2026. Both changes touch firmware variables on nearly every Windows PC with Secure Boot, so they were staged over years. (This is separate from the April 2026 removal of trust for cross-signed kernel drivers, which concerns driver signing, not boot.)

Read this lesson as a worked example of every idea so far: db, dbx, KEK-signed updates, certificate revocation, SVN, and the cost of breaking old media.

**The certificates** (Microsoft KB5062710, [Windows Secure Boot certificate expiration and CA updates](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/servicing/os/secure-boot/2025/06/windows-secure-boot-certificate-expiration-and-ca-updates)):

- Microsoft Corporation KEK CA 2011, in KEK, signs db and dbx updates: expires 24 June 2026; replaced by Microsoft Corporation KEK 2K CA 2023.
- Microsoft UEFI CA 2011, in db, signs third-party boot loaders and option ROMs: expires 27 June 2026; replaced by **two** certificates, Microsoft UEFI CA 2023 (boot loaders) and Microsoft Option ROM UEFI CA 2023 (option ROMs), so a system can trust option ROMs without trusting third-party loaders.
- Microsoft Windows Production PCA 2011, in db, signs the Windows boot loader: expires 19 October 2026; replaced by Windows UEFI CA 2023.

**Expiry is not revocation.** Microsoft rolls the 2023 certificates out automatically to most Windows devices. Devices without them keep starting after expiry, but get no new boot managers, db or dbx updates, or boot-level fixes.

blocks.title: CVE-2023-24932 phases and cert expiry (months from Jan 2023)

scenes.caption: May 2023: the initial deployment, with manual steps. July 2023: a second phase with simpler steps. Both were later superseded.

April 2024, evaluation: three controls replace the 2023 ones. Add Windows UEFI CA 2023 to db, install a 2023-signed boot manager, add PCA 2011 to dbx. An interlock stops them being applied out of order.
July 2024, deployment: the SVN mechanism arrives. Organisations are told to deploy the steps in order and update media.

June 2026: KEK CA 2011 and UEFI CA 2011 expire. October 2026: Windows Production PCA 2011 expires. Enforcement, which makes the PCA 2011 revocation automatic, had no date as of the article's September 2026 revision.

blocks.md:
**The four steps** in KB5025885, and the Windows event that confirms each (event details in Microsoft's KB5016061):

1. Add the Windows UEFI CA 2023 certificate to db: event **1036**.
2. Install the boot manager signed by Windows UEFI CA 2023: event **1799**.
3. Add Windows Production PCA 2011 to dbx, distrusting every boot manager it signed: event **1037**. Microsoft explains why it changed approach: instead of trying to list every vulnerable boot manager, untrusting the certificate is "a more reliable method".
4. Write the new SVN floor to firmware: event **1042**.

Step 3 cannot be undone while Secure Boot stays on; KB5025885 warns that even reformatting the disk will not remove applied revocations. Known issues it lists show why staging matters: some firmware fails to apply db or dbx updates; VMware VMs with Secure Boot failed to boot after the mitigations; some devices went into BitLocker recovery, so recovery keys must be backed up first; recovery and install media must be rebuilt with 2023-signed boot files.

blocks.code:
# Windows, read-only checks from KB5025885 (run as Administrator).
# They only read the db and dbx variables; nothing is written.
[System.Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetString((Get-SecureBootUEFI db).bytes) -match 'Windows UEFI CA 2023'
[System.Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetString((Get-SecureBootUEFI dbx).bytes) -match 'Microsoft Windows Production PCA 2011'
blocks.caption: Shown for reference, not run in this course. True on the first line means the new CA is trusted; True on the second means the old PCA is revoked. Fleet tools usually collect the same facts plus events 1036, 1799, 1037 and 1042.

blocks.md: Linux fleets see the same rollover from the other side: fwupd's HSI check `org.fwupd.hsi.Uefi.Db` reports whether the Microsoft UEFI CA 2023 is installed, because distribution shims signed only under the new CA will not boot on machines that lack it.

blocks.question: A kiosk PC never received the 2023 certificates. What happens after the 2011 certificates expire in 2026, according to Microsoft?
options: It stops booting immediately
Secure Boot switches itself off
It keeps booting, but can no longer receive new boot manager, db, dbx and boot-level security updates
The TPM is cleared
blocks.explain: Expiry does not stop the existing chain from booting. The device simply falls off the update path, so future boot-level fixes never reach it.

blocks.question: Why did Microsoft add the PCA 2011 certificate to dbx instead of continuing to add hashes of vulnerable boot managers?
options: Listing every vulnerable boot manager by hash was unreliable and costly; revoking the CA distrusts all of them at once
Hashes cannot be stored in dbx
The certificate had already expired
To free space in db
blocks.explain: Hash revocation misses rebuilds and consumes dbx space. Distrusting the signing certificate catches every boot manager it signed, at the cost of requiring a newly signed boot manager and updated media.

lessons.title: Measured boot: PCRs, extend and what each PCR records

blocks.md:
Plain idea: Secure Boot *blocks* what is not allowed. **Measured boot** *records* what actually ran, in a way the running software cannot rewrite, so that someone else can check it later. The two are complementary: Secure Boot can be bypassed silently, as BlackLotus showed, but a faithful record of the bypass cannot be erased afterwards.

The recorder is the **TPM** (Trusted Platform Module), a small security chip or firmware component specified by the TCG (Trusted Computing Group, the industry body that publishes the TPM and measurement specifications). Inside it are **PCRs** (Platform Configuration Registers). A PCR cannot be written; it can only be **extended**. Microsoft's documentation gives the rule ([Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/hardware-security/tpm/switch-pcr-banks-on-tpm-2-0-devices)):

blocks.caption: H is the bank's hash (SHA-256 in a SHA-256 bank) and the double bar means concatenation. PCRs 0 to 15 start at zero and reset only when the TPM itself resets, that is, at platform reset.

blocks.md:
Three consequences follow from that one line:

- **No undo.** To reach a given PCR value you must extend exactly the same digests in exactly the same order from reset. Software that runs later cannot remove an earlier measurement.
- **Order matters.** Extending A then B gives a different value from B then A.
- **Measure before you run.** Each stage measures the *next* stage before handing over control. A bootkit that runs can stop measuring things after itself, but the measurement of the bootkit itself is already in the PCR. That is why the stage doing the measuring must be trusted: lesson 12 is about anchoring it in hardware.

blocks.code:
import hashlib
sha = lambda b: hashlib.sha256(b).digest()

def extend(pcr, data):
    # PCR[N] = H(PCR[N] || digest of the measured thing)
    return sha(pcr + sha(data))

def boot(components):
    pcr = bytes(32)                      # reset value: 32 zero bytes
    for c in components:
        pcr = extend(pcr, c)
        print(f"  extend {c.decode():24} PCR now {pcr.hex()[:12]}")
    return pcr

print("clean boot (PCR4):")
a = boot([b"bootmgfw.efi (signed)", b"winload.efi"])
print("bootkit inserted first (PCR4):")
b = boot([b"grubx64.efi (bootkit)", b"bootmgfw.efi (signed)", b"winload.efi"])
print("same final PCR?", a == b)
blocks.caption: Runnable simulation of extend with SHA-256 (no TPM is used). The component names stand in for image hashes; real PCR4 also receives separator and action events, left out here.

blocks.code:
clean boot (PCR4):
  extend bootmgfw.efi (signed)    PCR now 8f35a3397b89
  extend winload.efi              PCR now fbebf131bdcb
bootkit inserted first (PCR4):
  extend grubx64.efi (bootkit)    PCR now e82e38f15714
  extend bootmgfw.efi (signed)    PCR now 2331a7771494
  extend winload.efi              PCR now 2acede7833f1
same final PCR? False
blocks.caption: Real output. Inserting one stage at the front changes every later value, so the final PCR differs even though the familiar files are still there.

blocks.title: PCR4 after each extend (first 6 hex digits, from pcr.py)

scenes.caption: Both boots start from the reset value: all zeros.
Clean boot: the boot manager is measured, then winload. Final value fbebf1...
Bootkit boot: grubx64.efi is measured first, so even the identical boot manager measurement now yields 2331a7 instead of 8f35a3.
Final 2acede... differs from fbebf1... No later code can extend its way back to the clean value.

blocks.md:
**What each PCR records** on a PC is fixed by the TCG PC Client Platform Firmware Profile, PFP 1.06 ([TCG PFP](https://medias.cdn.trustedcomputinggroup.org/production/TCG_PC_Client_Platform_Firmware_Profile_Version_1_06_Revision_52_pub_3_1184065dfc.pdf), Table 1):

- PCR0: the SRTM (Static Root of Trust for Measurement), BIOS code, embedded option ROMs and PI drivers
- PCR1: platform configuration; PCR2: UEFI driver and application code; PCR3: their configuration and data
- PCR4: UEFI boot manager code and boot attempts, which is where boot applications such as `bootmgfw.efi` are measured
- PCR5: boot manager configuration and the GPT (GUID Partition Table, the disk's partition layout); PCR6: manufacturer specific
- PCR7: **Secure Boot policy**: the SecureBoot variable, PK, KEK, db, dbx and the db entry used to verify each loaded image
- PCRs 8 to 15: for the OS

blocks.title: Which PCRs each event type may extend (TCG PFP 1.06)

scenes.caption: EV_SEPARATOR goes into PCRs 0 to 7. It marks the point where firmware hands over the measurement process, so anything measured afterwards is clearly the OS side.
Boot applications (EV_EFI_BOOT_SERVICES_APPLICATION) go to PCR2 or PCR4. A new or changed bootloader on the ESP shows up in PCR4.
Secure Boot variables (VARIABLE_DRIVER_CONFIG) and the db entry that authorised each image (VARIABLE_AUTHORITY) land in PCR7. A dbx update or a turned-off Secure Boot changes PCR7.

blocks.md: **Sealing** uses this. A key can be sealed so the TPM releases it only if chosen PCRs hold the same values as when it was sealed. BitLocker seals the disk key this way; that is why ESET saw BlackLotus suspend BitLocker before changing the boot chain, and why KB5025885 warns that applying the dbx and boot manager changes can trigger BitLocker recovery. Changing what is measured changes the PCRs, and the sealed key stays locked.

Misconception: "The TPM checks the boot." It does not decide anything. It only stores what firmware and loaders tell it. Enforcement comes from Secure Boot, from sealing, or from a remote verifier reading the values (lesson 11).

blocks.question: Secure Boot is switched off in the setup menu, and nothing else changes. Which PCR is designed to reveal this?
options: PCR0
PCR4
PCR7
PCR12
blocks.explain: PFP 1.06 requires the SecureBoot variable and the PK, KEK, db and dbx contents to be measured into PCR7, the Secure Boot policy PCR.

blocks.question: Malware running in the kernel wants PCR4 to hold the clean value fbebf1... again. Why can it not do that?
options: PCR4 is encrypted
The kernel cannot talk to the TPM
PCR4 is reset by every dbx update
It can only extend, and no sequence of further extends returns to an earlier value without a TPM reset, which means a reboot
blocks.explain: Extend is one-way: the new value hashes the old one. Reaching a target value would require finding a hash preimage. Only a platform reset clears PCRs 0 to 15, and then the boot is measured again from scratch.

lessons.title: Replaying a TCG event log to catch a lie

blocks.md:
Plain idea: a PCR is a single hash. It tells you *whether* the boot matched, never *what* ran. The **event log** says what ran: each time firmware extends a PCR, it also appends an entry describing the measurement. The Linux kernel documentation quotes the TCG on how the two fit ([kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/security/tpm/tpm_event_log.html)): the measurement log is not trusted on its own, but it carries much richer information than the PCRs, and the PCR contents are used to validate it.

So a verifier **replays** the log: start every PCR at zero, extend each logged digest in order, and compare the result with the PCR values the TPM reports. If they match, the log is a faithful explanation. If not, someone lost, added or edited an entry.

**The entry format.** PFP 1.06 defines every entry after the first as a `TCG_PCR_EVENT2`, little-endian:

- `pcrIndex` (4 bytes) and `eventType` (4 bytes), for example `0x80000003` EV_EFI_BOOT_SERVICES_APPLICATION or `0x00000004` EV_SEPARATOR
- `digests`: a count, then for each PCR bank a 2-byte algorithm id (`0x000B` is SHA-256) and the digest
- `eventSize` (4 bytes) and the event data: a variable name and value, a device path, or a separator value

The first entry is special: an EV_NO_ACTION "Specification ID" event, stored in an older fixed-size layout, which tells parsers the log version and which digest algorithms and sizes follow. EV_NO_ACTION entries are never extended into any PCR.

blocks.code:
import hashlib, struct
sha = lambda b: hashlib.sha256(b).digest()
SEP, VAR, APP = 0x4, 0x80000001, 0x80000003
NAMES = {SEP: "EV_SEPARATOR", VAR: "EV_EFI_VARIABLE_DRIVER_CONFIG",
         APP: "EV_EFI_BOOT_SERVICES_APPLICATION"}

def event(pcr, etype, data):     # one TCG_PCR_EVENT2, SHA-256 bank (0x000B) only
    return (struct.pack("<IIIH", pcr, etype, 1, 0x000B) + sha(data)
            + struct.pack("<I", len(data)) + data)

def parse(log):
    off = 0
    while off < len(log):
        pcr, etype, count, alg = struct.unpack_from("<IIIH", log, off)
        digest = log[off + 14:off + 46]
        size, = struct.unpack_from("<I", log, off + 46)
        data = log[off + 50:off + 50 + size]
        off += 50 + size
        yield pcr, etype, digest, data

def replay(log):
    pcrs = {}
    for pcr, etype, digest, data in parse(log):
        pcrs[pcr] = sha(pcrs.get(pcr, bytes(32)) + digest)
    return pcrs

sep = bytes(4)
real = (event(7, VAR, b"SecureBoot=01") + event(7, VAR, b"dbx v3")
        + event(7, SEP, sep) + event(4, SEP, sep)
        + event(4, APP, b"grubx64.efi")          # the bootkit ran
        + event(4, APP, b"bootmgfw.efi"))
tpm = replay(real)                   # what the TPM really holds
for pcr, etype, d, data in parse(real):
    print(f"PCR{pcr} {NAMES[etype]:33} {data!r}")

edited = real.replace(event(4, APP, b"grubx64.efi"), b"")  # log edited on disk
for name, log in [("real log", real), ("edited log", edited)]:
    r = replay(log)
    print(name, {p: "match" if r[p] == tpm[p] else "MISMATCH" for p in (4, 7)})
blocks.caption: Runnable parser and replayer for a synthetic log in the TCG_PCR_EVENT2 layout, SHA-256 bank only. Simplified: no Spec ID header, and each digest is the hash of the short event data instead of an image hash.

blocks.code:
PCR7 EV_EFI_VARIABLE_DRIVER_CONFIG     b'SecureBoot=01'
PCR7 EV_EFI_VARIABLE_DRIVER_CONFIG     b'dbx v3'
PCR7 EV_SEPARATOR                      b'\x00\x00\x00\x00'
PCR4 EV_SEPARATOR                      b'\x00\x00\x00\x00'
PCR4 EV_EFI_BOOT_SERVICES_APPLICATION  b'grubx64.efi'
PCR4 EV_EFI_BOOT_SERVICES_APPLICATION  b'bootmgfw.efi'
real log {4: 'match', 7: 'match'}
edited log {4: 'MISMATCH', 7: 'match'}
blocks.caption: Real output. The honest log explains both PCRs. The edited log, with the bootkit's own entry deleted, no longer explains PCR4, while PCR7 still matches because nothing about Secure Boot policy changed.

blocks.title: What the verifier does with the edited log

scenes.caption: Start: the verifier holds the TPM's signed PCR values and a log file copied from the disk, which the bootkit was able to edit.
Replay folds each logged digest into a running PCR value, exactly as the TPM did at boot.
PCR7 replays to the TPM's value: the Secure Boot policy entries are intact.
PCR4 does not: the deleted grubx64.efi digest is still inside the real PCR. The verifier cannot see what was removed, only that the log is lying.
scenes.output: alert: log does not explain PCR4

blocks.prompt: The attacker cannot edit the log without breaking the replay. What else could they try, and does it work?
blocks.reveal: They could leave the log honest and hope nobody reads it, which is why Microsoft's BlackLotus guidance tells responders to diff the logs in `C:\Windows\Logs\MeasuredBoot` across boots. Or they could stop measurements from happening at all, by compromising the code that measures. fwupd even has an HSI check for firmware that leaves some of PCRs 0 to 7 empty, because a local attacker could then extend fake values into them. A trustworthy measurement needs a trustworthy measurer.

blocks.md: On Linux, `tpm2_eventlog` from tpm2-tools parses a binary event log in this format, and fwupd's HSI check `Tpm.ReconstructionPcr0` replays the PCR0 entries and compares them with the TPM. Both only read.

blocks.question: A replayed log matches every PCR the TPM reports. What exactly have you learned?
options: The machine is free of malware
The log is a faithful record of what was measured during this boot; whether those things are good is a separate policy check
Secure Boot was on
The firmware has no bugs
blocks.explain: A match proves the log explains the PCRs. You still have to read the entries and compare them against known-good values, and you are trusting that the measuring code measured honestly.

blocks.question: Why is an EV_NO_ACTION entry skipped during replay?
options: PFP 1.06 says it must not extend any PCR; it carries informative data only
It is encrypted
It belongs to PCR 23
It is always corrupt
blocks.explain: EV_NO_ACTION records information, such as the Specification ID header, that was never extended. Folding it into a replay would produce wrong PCR values.

lessons.title: Remote attestation: quotes, nonces and what a verifier can trust

blocks.md: Plain idea: an infected machine cannot be trusted to report its own health. Microsoft's measured boot documentation says this directly: PCs infected with rootkits can appear healthy even with anti-malware running, so you cannot trust the client to tell you whether it is healthy ([Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/operating-system-security/system-security/secure-the-windows-10-boot-process)). **Remote attestation** lets the TPM vouch for the PCRs instead.

The pieces:

- A **quote**: the TPM signs a digest of selected PCR values with an **attestation key** whose private half never leaves the TPM. The tpm2-tools manual describes `tpm2_quote` as producing exactly this signed structure ([tpm2_quote](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tpm2-software/tpm2-tools/master/man/tpm2_quote.1.md)).
- A **nonce** (a number used once): fresh random data from the verifier, included in what the TPM signs. The manual: qualifying data "is typically used to add a nonce against replay attacks".
- The **event log**, sent alongside, replayed as in lesson 10.
- A **policy**: the verifier's list of acceptable values (known boot managers, expected dbx version, Secure Boot on).

scenes.caption: The verifier picks a fresh random nonce and asks the host for a quote over PCRs 0 to 7.
The agent passes the request to the TPM. The agent itself may be compromised; it never sees the attestation key.
The TPM signs the PCR digest together with N and returns it.
The agent forwards the quote and the event log. It can drop or delay them, but cannot forge the signature.
The verifier checks the signature, checks that N is the nonce it just sent, replays the log, compares it to policy, then decides: full network, quarantine or investigate.

blocks.code:
import hmac, hashlib, os
# Toy: an HMAC with a key only the "TPM" holds stands in for the
# attestation key's signature over (PCR digest, nonce).
AK = os.urandom(32)
def tpm_quote(pcr_digest, nonce):
    return pcr_digest, nonce, hmac.new(AK, pcr_digest + nonce, "sha256").digest()

GOOD = hashlib.sha256(b"known-good PCR0-7").digest()
EVIL = hashlib.sha256(b"PCR0-7 with bootkit").digest()

def check_bad(q, nonce):             # BUG: never compares the nonce
    d, n, sig = q
    ok = hmac.compare_digest(sig, hmac.new(AK, d + n, "sha256").digest())
    return ok and d == GOOD

def check_good(q, nonce):
    d, n, sig = q
    ok = hmac.compare_digest(sig, hmac.new(AK, d + n, "sha256").digest())
    return ok and n == nonce and d == GOOD

monday = os.urandom(16)
saved = tpm_quote(GOOD, monday)      # recorded while the machine was clean
# Tuesday: machine now boots a bootkit; the verifier sends a fresh nonce
tuesday = os.urandom(16)
honest = tpm_quote(EVIL, tuesday)    # what the TPM would sign today
for name, q in [("fresh honest quote", honest), ("replayed Monday quote", saved)]:
    print(f"{name:22} bad={check_bad(q, tuesday)!s:5} good={check_good(q, tuesday)}")
blocks.caption: Toy model: an HMAC with a key only the 'TPM' function holds stands in for the attestation key's signature, so this runs with the standard library. The nonce check is the point.

blocks.code:
fresh honest quote     bad=False good=False
replayed Monday quote  bad=True  good=False
blocks.caption: Real output. An infected host replays Monday's genuine quote. The verifier that skips the nonce check accepts it; the fixed verifier rejects it, and the honest fresh quote fails policy as it should.

blocks.md: Freshness is part of the claim. A valid signature over good PCRs only proves the machine was good *at some point*. The nonce binds the quote to this request.

**What attestation cannot do.** Cloudflare's write-up on its server fleet makes the limit explicit: a TPM is not an on-path security mechanism; firmware is responsible for doing the measurements, and a tampered firmware could extend measurements that a remote attestor accepts but that do not represent what was loaded ([Cloudflare](https://blog.cloudflare.com/anchoring-trust-a-hardware-secure-boot-story/)). The first measurement must come from code an attacker cannot change, which is what the hardware roots of trust in the next lesson provide.

**Practical uses.** Conditional network access for laptops, admitting servers to a cluster only if they booted the expected image, and releasing secrets (disk keys, workload credentials) only to machines whose PCRs match. Microsoft notes that Windows provides the measured boot interfaces but that the attestation client and server come from other tools.

**Defender view.** Alert on quotes that fail replay, on PCR7 changes outside a planned dbx or certificate rollout, and on new PCR4 boot applications.

blocks.question: A verifier accepts any validly signed quote whose PCRs match policy, without sending a nonce. What can a host infected today do?
options: Nothing, signatures cannot be copied
Forge the attestation key
Reset PCR7 to zero
Send a genuine quote it saved before infection, which still verifies
blocks.explain: Without a nonce, an old quote is indistinguishable from a new one. The signature is genuine; it just describes the past.

blocks.question: Why is a TPM quote less useful if the firmware code that performs the first measurements can be modified by an attacker?
options: The TPM stops working
Quotes become unsigned
The modified code can measure what the verifier expects instead of what actually ran
PCR7 is cleared
blocks.explain: The TPM records whatever it is told. If the measurer lies, the quote faithfully signs the lie. Anchoring the first measurement in immutable hardware addresses this.

lessons.title: Hardware roots of trust: Boot Guard, AMD PSB and Apple silicon

blocks.md:
Plain idea: UEFI Secure Boot is enforced *by the firmware*, so it cannot protect the firmware itself. A **hardware root of trust** moves the very first check into something an attacker cannot rewrite: CPU microcode, a boot ROM, or one-time-programmable **fuses** (on-chip bits that can be written once and never changed). That first check verifies the first block of the firmware before the main CPU runs it.

ESET's corrected LoJax advice says exactly this: to protect against tampering with the SPI flash, the root of trust must move to hardware, and Intel Boot Guard on a properly configured machine would have refused to boot after the compromise.

blocks.title: Three hardware-anchored chains (what each first step verifies)

nodes.label:
Initial boot block
(OEM key in fuses)

scenes.caption: Intel Boot Guard: microcode authenticates Intel's ACM, which checks the firmware's initial boot block against the OEM key programmed into fuses at manufacture.
AMD PSB: the Platform Security Processor, an Arm core inside the chip, boots from its own ROM and authenticates the first BIOS block before releasing the x86 cores from reset.
Apple silicon: the Boot ROM starts the chain, LLB verifies signatures and loads the LocalPolicy, then iBoot and the kernel follow.
Same shape in all three: an immutable first step, a vendor or OEM key the attacker cannot change, and verification before execution.

blocks.md: **Intel Boot Guard.** Introduced with 4th-generation Core processors (Haswell, 2013). A UEFI Forum white paper by Vincent Zimmer and Michael Krau of Intel describes three modes, verified boot, measured boot, or both, with verified boot used by most OEMs; the OEM's public key is programmed into field-programmable fuses during manufacturing and cannot be updated afterwards ([UEFI Forum white paper](https://www.UEFI.org/sites/default/files/resources/UEFI%20RoT%20white%20paper_Final%208%208%2016%20%28003%29.pdf)). Intel's documents call the verifying code an **ACM** (Authenticated Code Module): firmware authenticated by microcode and run from internal cache. Boot profiles differ in **enforcement policy** (what happens if the firmware fails verification) and **measurement policy** (whether it is also measured into the TPM).

**AMD PSB** (Platform Secure Boot), as Cloudflare describes it: authenticates the first block of BIOS/UEFI before releasing the x86 CPUs from reset, authenticates the ROM on every boot (not only during updates), and is configured by one-time-programmable fuses such as the platform vendor ID and a BIOS key revision used for anti-rollback. There is no way back from a fused CPU, and if validation fails the x86 cores stay locked.

**Apple silicon Macs.** Apple's Platform Security guide: the chip runs Boot ROM code first, then the Low-Level Bootloader (**LLB**) verifies signatures, loads firmware for on-chip controllers, and loads the **LocalPolicy**, a file signed by the Secure Enclave that records whether this OS is set to Full, Reduced or Permissive Security. An anti-replay value checked against Secure Enclave storage stops an attacker restoring an older, weaker LocalPolicy. In Full Security only software known to be the latest at install time boots ([Apple](https://support.apple.com/guide/security/boot-process-for-a-mac-with-apple-silicon-secac71d5623/web)).

**What these do not cover.** They verify only the code region they are set to cover: Binarly's LogoFAIL research (next lesson) showed logos read from the ESP or NVRAM lie outside what Boot Guard or AMD's Hardware-Validated Boot verifies. And they rely on the OEM's key staying secret: Binarly reported in 2023 that Boot Guard keys leaked in the MSI breach and in leaked Intel platform code, and that Intel and Supermicro devices shared one.

Hardware roots of trust are only as good as their configuration. Boot Guard and PSB both depend on the OEM fusing a key and choosing an enforcing policy; a board shipped unfused or with a measure-only policy gets little protection.

Check without changing anything: fwupd's HSI report has `IntelBootguard.Enabled`, `IntelBootguard.Verified`, `IntelBootguard.Otp`, `Amd.PlatformSecureBoot` and `Amd.RollbackProtection`. Do not run vendor fusing or policy tools on a machine to find out; fuses are permanent.

blocks.question: LoJax wrote a modified firmware image into SPI flash. On a machine with Intel Boot Guard in verified mode with the OEM key fused, what would most likely happen at the next boot?
options: Secure Boot would catch the new DXE driver
The ACM would find the firmware's initial boot block no longer verifies against the OEM key, and the policy would stop the boot
Nothing, Boot Guard only measures
The TPM would erase the implant
blocks.explain: ESET states that with Boot Guard available and properly configured, the machine would have refused to boot after the compromise. Secure Boot, which runs inside the modified firmware, would not.

blocks.question: A data-centre team buys used servers whose AMD CPUs were fused for another vendor's firmware key with PSB. What should they expect?
options: The CPUs will only boot firmware signed with that vendor's key, because PSB fuses cannot be undone
The CPUs reset to factory state on first boot
PSB turns itself off
Only Secure Boot is affected
blocks.explain: Cloudflare notes there is no way to roll a fused CPU back to unfused. PSB binds the processor to the OEM's firmware signing key, which is the security property and also the resale catch.

lessons.title: Case: LogoFAIL, a boot logo parsed by the most trusted code

blocks.md:
Plain idea: firmware is software, and software that parses attacker-controlled files has parsing bugs. On 6 December 2023 the Binarly REsearch Team presented **LogoFAIL** at Black Hat Europe: the image parsers that draw the manufacturer's logo during boot, shipped by all three major IBVs (Independent BIOS Vendors: AMI, Insyde and Phoenix, who write the firmware base most PC makers customise), were full of memory-safety bugs ([Binarly](https://www.binarly.io/blog/finding-logofail-dangers-of-image-parsing-system-boot), [CERT/CC VU#811862](https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/811862)).

Why it matters: the parsers run in the DXE phase, before the OS, in C code that Binarly describes as having few or no exploit mitigations. Recall the prereq course on exploit mitigations: none of ASLR, canaries or CFI can help code that does not have them.

**The attack surface.** Normally the logo sits in a signed firmware volume. But many OEMs let users customise it, and Binarly found the logo read from: a fixed path on the ESP; an NVRAM variable naming an ESP path; an NVRAM variable holding the compressed image; or a vendor tool that patches a firmware update capsule. CERT/CC: an attacker with local privileged access can exploit these. Because the logo is read from outside the region Intel Boot Guard or AMD Hardware-Validated Boot verifies, those features do not protect it, and Secure Boot checks executables, not picture files.

**The numbers.** Fuzzing (feeding a program huge numbers of generated malformed inputs and watching for crashes) found 29 unique crashes across BMP, GIF, JPEG, PCX, PNG and TGA parsers, 15 judged exploitable. Three CVEs track the vendor code: CVE-2023-39539 (AMI), CVE-2023-40238 (Insyde), CVE-2023-5058 (Phoenix). NVD describes CVE-2023-40238 as an integer signedness error in the Insyde BMP decoder's RLE4/RLE8 handling, fixed in specific InsydeH2O kernel versions.

blocks.title: One bug class Binarly showed: a 32-bit allocation size that wraps

scenes.caption: A normal 640 by 480 logo: row = 1280 bytes, size = 614,400 bytes. Allocation and decoded data agree.
A crafted header sets width = 0x80000200. Doubling it needs 33 bits, so 32-bit arithmetic wraps to 0x400: a 1 KiB buffer.
The decoder still writes data for the declared width into that 1 KiB buffer: a heap overflow inside firmware, before any OS defence exists.
Fix, part 1: refuse dimensions no screen needs. Part 2: compute in wide arithmetic and refuse anything that does not fit, instead of letting it wrap.

blocks.caption: Toy model in Python: the & U32 mask imitates C's uint32 wrap-around. Runnable, touches no firmware. The example width 0x80000200 is the one Binarly's write-up uses to explain the AMI PNG bug.

blocks.code:
width=0x280: writes 0x96000 bytes, bad alloc=0x96000, good=0x96000
width=0x80000200: writes 0x100000400 bytes, bad alloc=0x400, good=refuse: dimensions out of range
blocks.caption: Real output. The vulnerable path asks for 0x400 bytes while the decoder will produce 0x100000400 bytes; the fixed path refuses the image.

blocks.md: Every parser in firmware is attack surface with the highest privilege on the machine. The fix is the same as anywhere else (validate sizes, use checked arithmetic, fuzz), plus the firmware-specific rule: do not read customisable data from places the verified boot chain does not cover.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: install the firmware updates OEMs released after the advisories; turn off logo customisation where the setup menu allows it. *Detect*: new or changed image files on the ESP and unexpected changes to logo-related NVRAM variables are signals; measured boot may not show them, because picture files are data, not code. *Respond*: treat a firmware-level compromise as requiring a clean reflash from the vendor's image.

A year later the bug class reappeared in practice: Bootkitty, the first UEFI bootkit for Linux, was analysed by ESET in November 2024 as a proof of concept ([ESET](https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/bootkitty-analyzing-first-uefi-bootkit-linux/)); ESET later traced it to a student project in Korea's Best of the Best (BoB) training programme. Binarly then reported that Bootkitty carried an exploit for the Insyde BMP bug CVE-2023-40238 that injected certificates into `MokList`.

blocks.question: Why did Secure Boot not stop LogoFAIL?
options: Secure Boot was disabled on all affected devices
Secure Boot verifies executables before running them; a logo is data parsed by already-trusted firmware code
The logos were signed by Microsoft
Secure Boot only runs after the OS starts
blocks.explain: The vulnerable code is the trusted firmware itself. Feeding it malicious data needs no unsigned executable, so nothing for Secure Boot to reject.

blocks.question: A vendor fixes the overflow by checking `if (width * 2 < width) reject;` in uint32 arithmetic, and also multiplies by height later without a check. Is the fix complete?
options: Yes, the doubling was the only overflow
Yes, because height is always small
No, because the check itself always rejects
No: row times height can still wrap; every multiplication feeding a size needs a range or overflow check
blocks.explain: The toy shows two multiplications. Checking one leaves the other. Bounding width and height first, then computing in a wider type, closes both.

lessons.title: Trusting the wrong things: PKfail and CVE-2024-7344

blocks.md:
Plain idea: Secure Boot's maths can be perfect and the system still fail, if the trusted key is not secret or the trusted program does not do the checking it was trusted to do. Two cases, one of each.

**PKfail (July 2024).** Binarly found that many production devices shipped with a **test** Platform Key from AMI's reference code, a key meant to be replaced by each device maker ([Binarly](https://www.binarly.io/blog/pkfail-untrusted-platform-keys-undermine-secure-boot), [CERT/CC VU#455367](https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/455367)). The certificates even said so: issuers containing "DO NOT TRUST" or "DO NOT SHIP". Binarly found the private half of one such key in a leak: a suspected ODM (original design manufacturer, the company that builds hardware other brands sell) employee had published source code on a public GitHub repository, with the key in an encrypted file protected by a 4-character password. The issue is tracked as CVE-2024-8105.

Binarly's numbers: more than 10% of the firmware images in its dataset used an untrusted Platform Key (8% of those released in the last four years); 22 unique untrusted keys; the first affected firmware dated from May 2012 and the latest from June 2024; an advisory listing almost 900 device models. Lesson 4 explains the impact: whoever holds the PK private key can rewrite KEK, db and dbx, and so sign any bootkit.

CERT/CC's root-cause line is worth remembering: UEFI key verification only checks keys against the local database, with no programmatic safeguard that stops a key marked "DO NOT TRUST" from shipping.

**Fix and check.** Device makers must generate and guard their own PK, for example in an HSM (Hardware Security Module, a device that keeps private keys inside it), and ship firmware updates replacing test keys. Fleets can check today: fwupd's HSI test `Uefi.Pk` fails if a test key such as "DO NOT TRUST - AMI Test PK" is enrolled.

blocks.code:
# Audit a fleet inventory for test Platform Keys (synthetic data).
# A real inventory would come from your management agent or fwupd.
MARKERS = ("DO NOT TRUST", "DO NOT SHIP", "TEST")

fleet = [
    {"host": "lab-01",  "pk_subject": "CN=Contoso Platform Key 2024",
     "pk_issuer": "CN=Contoso Platform Key 2024"},
    {"host": "lab-02",  "pk_subject": "CN=DO NOT TRUST - AMI Test PK",
     "pk_issuer": "CN=DO NOT TRUST - AMI Test PK"},
    {"host": "lab-03",  "pk_subject": "CN=Contoso Platform Key 2024",
     "pk_issuer": "CN=Contoso Platform Key 2024"},
    {"host": "kiosk-9", "pk_subject": None, "pk_issuer": None},
]

def classify(m):
    if m["pk_subject"] is None:
        return "NO PK: setup mode, key databases writable without a signature"
    text = (m["pk_subject"] + " " + m["pk_issuer"]).upper()
    if any(k in text for k in MARKERS):
        return "TEST KEY: anyone with the leaked key can rewrite KEK, db, dbx"
    return "ok"

for m in fleet:
    print(f"{m['host']:8} {classify(m)}")
blocks.caption: Toy inventory audit on synthetic data. In a real fleet the PK certificate subject and issuer come from your endpoint agent or from fwupd; reading them changes nothing.

blocks.code:
lab-01   ok
lab-02   TEST KEY: anyone with the leaked key can rewrite KEK, db, dbx
lab-03   ok
kiosk-9  NO PK: setup mode, key databases writable without a signature
blocks.caption: Real output. The rule is deliberately simple: a test marker in the PK certificate, or no PK at all, is a finding.

blocks.title: How a test key travels from reference code to your desk

scenes.caption: The IBV's reference code carries a test Platform Key, labelled untrusted, expecting downstream builders to replace it.
The key is never replaced and ships in products of unrelated brands, client and server alike. Binarly saw the same keys across vendors.
One private key leaks through published source. Every device enrolled with it now trusts whatever its holder signs.

blocks.md: **CVE-2024-7344 (January 2025).** ESET found a UEFI application in recovery software from several vendors (Howyar Technologies and others) signed under Microsoft's third-party UEFI CA 2011. Instead of the firmware's `LoadImage` and `StartImage` functions, which enforce Secure Boot, it used its own PE loader, so it would run any binary, even unsigned, from a file it read at boot ([ESET](https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/under-cloak-uefi-secure-boot-introducing-cve-2024-7344/)). Every UEFI system with Microsoft third-party UEFI signing enabled was affected; ESET notes Windows 11 Secured-core PCs should have that option disabled by default. ESET reported it through CERT/CC in mid-2024; Microsoft revoked the vulnerable binaries in the January 14, 2025 Patch Tuesday update.

blocks.caption: Toy model of the bug class, not of the real product: a trusted program that loads the next stage itself instead of handing it to the firmware's verifying loader.

blocks.code:
vendor-recovery-v2 bad: running vendor-recovery-v2 good: running vendor-recovery-v2
unsigned-payload   bad: running unsigned-payload   good: Secure Boot violation
blocks.caption: Real output. Both loaders run the allowed image; only the fixed one refuses the unsigned payload.

blocks.md: A signature vouches for who built a program, not for what it does. Any signed boot component that loads code must pass that code back through the platform's verification, or it becomes a hole in the chain for every machine that trusts its signer.

blocks.question: A laptop's PK certificate issuer reads 'DO NOT TRUST - AMI Test PK', and Secure Boot shows as enabled. What is the risk?
options: Anyone holding that test key's private half can enrol their own KEK and db entries and boot code of their choice
None, Secure Boot is on
Only the logo can be changed
The TPM will refuse to start
blocks.explain: Secure Boot is enforcing, but against lists the attacker can rewrite. With a leaked or shared test PK, the trust anchor is not secret.

blocks.question: Why was CVE-2024-7344 fixed by revocation rather than only by a new version of the recovery software?
options: New versions cannot be signed
Revocation is cheaper than patching
The old signed binary would still be trusted and could be brought back by an attacker; it had to be distrusted in dbx
dbx updates also install the new version
