blocks.explain: Exactly the BlackLotus lesson: a vulnerable signed binary stays useful to attackers until the platform stops trusting it. Microsoft revoked the old binaries in January 2025.

lessons.title: Firmware implants in the wild: LoJax, MosaicRegressor, CosmicStrand

blocks.md: Plain idea: firmware implants are rare, but the few found in the wild share one design problem and one goal. The problem: the implant runs long before the OS exists, and its code is gone from memory by the time the OS runs. The goal: get a normal OS-level payload running on every boot. Each case solves the problem differently.

**LoJax (ESET, 27 September 2018).** Attributed with high confidence to the Sednit group (also known as APT28, Sofacy or Fancy Bear). The added DXE driver, SecDxe, registers a callback for the moment the firmware is about to start the OS loader. The callback loads an NTFS driver (one written by Hacking Team, a surveillance-software vendor whose internal files leaked in 2015), writes two files to the Windows partition, and changes a registry value so Windows runs the dropper early in startup. ESET found it modelled on Computrace/LoJack, an anti-theft product that legitimately ships as a firmware module so it survives reinstalls.

**MosaicRegressor (Kaspersky, 5 October 2020).** Called by Kaspersky the second known public case of malicious UEFI firmware in the wild ([Securelist](https://securelist.com/mosaicregressor/98849/)). Its four modules were based on Hacking Team's leaked VectorEDK bootkit code. They write `IntelUpdate.exe` into the Windows Startup folder and rewrite it if it is deleted. The wider MosaicRegressor framework hit diplomats and NGO members in Africa, Asia and Europe; only two of those victims also had the UEFI implant. The infection vector is unknown; Kaspersky considers physical access with a USB update tool possible.

**CosmicStrand (Kaspersky, 25 July 2022).** Found in firmware images of Gigabyte and ASUS motherboards built around the Intel H81 chipset ([Securelist](https://securelist.com/cosmicstrand-uefi-firmware-rootkit/106973/)). It is the clearest example of the hand-off problem: a patched firmware driver installs a hook, and each hook installs the next one at a later boot stage, until code reaches the Windows kernel. Kaspersky saw victims in China, Vietnam, Iran and Russia, all apparently private individuals, with one variant active around 2016 to 2017 and the current one in 2020. Qihoo 360, a Chinese security company, had described an early variant in 2017.

blocks.title: CosmicStrand's chain of hooks, as Kaspersky describes it

scenes.caption: Firmware phase: the attackers patched a legitimate driver so it redirects one UEFI boot service to their code, which waits for the Windows boot manager to be loaded.
Each stage plants a hook in the next component while it is still in memory: boot manager, then the Windows loader just before it hands over to the kernel.
Inside the kernel, the hook runs a payload that fetches more code from the network. Kaspersky notes it also attempts to disable PatchGuard, Windows' kernel integrity check.

blocks.md:
**What defenders can take from all three.**

- *How they were found*: by firmware scanners inside endpoint products (ESET's UEFI Scanner for LoJax, Kaspersky's Firmware Scanner for MosaicRegressor). Scanning the firmware image, not just the disk, is what catches this class.
- *Signals on the OS side*: new files appearing at boot in Startup folders or system directories with no installer event; registry boot entries changing; kernel code hooks; known flash-access drivers being loaded (LoJax).
- *Prevention*: SPI write protection configured and locked (lesson 3), a hardware root of trust verifying firmware (lesson 12), signed and anti-rollback firmware updates (lesson 16).
- *Response*: reflash the full firmware region from a vendor image, ideally with a hardware programmer, or replace the board; then rebuild the OS. ESET notes that a firmware update may remove such an implant if it rewrites the whole BIOS region.
Do not expect an OS reinstall, a disk wipe or an EDR clean-up to remove any of these three. All were designed precisely to survive them.

blocks.question: All three implants drop an ordinary Windows program or kernel payload rather than doing everything from firmware. Why?
options: Firmware cannot run code
Windows requires it
To avoid Secure Boot
Firmware code finishes before the OS runs, and a normal OS payload is easier to update, network-enable and keep running
blocks.explain: The implant's firmware stage lives only during boot. Handing off to a normal OS payload gives the attacker networking and flexibility, while the firmware stage guarantees it comes back.

blocks.question: A Kaspersky-style firmware scanner flags a board's SPI image as containing an unknown DXE driver. The OS looks clean. What is the right response?
options: Reflash the full firmware region from the vendor's known-good image (or replace the board), then rebuild the OS and investigate how write access was gained
Reinstall the OS
Clear the TPM
Turn Secure Boot off and on
blocks.explain: The implant lives in flash, so only rewriting the flash removes it. The investigation matters too: something had write access to the firmware.

lessons.title: Firmware updates, resilience and the BMC beside the CPU

blocks.md:
Plain idea: firmware must be updatable, or bugs like LogoFAIL could never be fixed. But the update path is also the most direct way to put new code into the flash. NIST's guidance turns this into rules: only authenticated images, no rollback to vulnerable versions, no way around the update path, and a way to recover when something goes wrong anyway.

**NIST SP 800-147, BIOS Protection Guidelines (April 2011)** ([NIST](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/147/final)) asks for four features:

- **Authenticated update**: every update image is digitally signed and verified with a key held by a **Root of Trust for Update (RTU)**, a protected verifier and key store.
- **Optional secure local update**: a physically present user may authorise an update, for example to recover a bricked board.
- **Integrity protection**: the firmware cannot be modified outside the authenticated update path (the job BIOSWE, BLE and SMM_BWP do in lesson 3).
- **Non-bypassability**: no component, including the CPU, can bypass the authenticated update mechanism.

It also says the authenticated update *should* prevent unauthorized rollback to an earlier authentic version with a known weakness, for example by checking that the new version number is higher, and lists rollback to an authentic but vulnerable image as a particularly insidious attack.

blocks.caption: Toy firmware-update verifier, runnable with the standard library. An HMAC stands in for the vendor's signature; installed_svn plays the role of a rollback counter in protected storage.

blocks.code:
forged 1.5 bad=False good=rejected: bad signature
old 1.2    bad=True  good=rejected: rollback below SVN 4
new 1.5    bad=True  good=installed
blocks.caption: Real output. The forged image fails the signature check in both versions. The old 1.2 image is authentic, so the vulnerable verifier installs it; the fixed verifier refuses because its security version is below the installed floor.

blocks.md:
**NIST SP 800-193, Platform Firmware Resiliency Guidelines (May 2018)** ([NIST](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/193/final)) widens the scope to all platform firmware and organises it around three principles:

- **Protection**: keep firmware and critical data in a state of integrity, including authenticated updates (the 800-147 idea, applied more widely).
- **Detection**: notice when firmware or critical data has been changed from an authorised state.
- **Recovery**: restore firmware and critical data to a good state when corruption is detected, or when an administrator forces it.

Each has a logical root of trust: **RTU** for update, **RTD** for detection, **RTRec** for recovery. AMD PSB's every-boot check (lesson 12) is detection; a board that keeps a known-good copy and falls back to it is recovery.

scenes.caption: Protection: an update reaches the flash only through the RTU, which checks the signature and refuses rollback below the security version.
Detection: on every boot the RTD verifies the flash contents, catching changes that bypassed the update path, for example a race like LoJax's.
Recovery: if verification fails, the RTRec restores a known-good image from protected storage instead of leaving a brick or an implant.

blocks.md: **The processors beside the CPU.** SP 800-193 points out that most servers and clients include a **BMC** (Baseboard Management Controller, on servers) or a **ME** (Management Engine, on clients): a separate processor with its own firmware for out-of-band management, so administrators can manage a machine without its OS running. CISA and NSA's joint guidance of 14 June 2023 describes BMCs as trusted components that run separately from the OS and firmware and allow remote control even when the system is shut down; weak credentials, missed firmware updates and flat networks leave them exposed, offering attackers a foothold with pre-boot execution potential ([CISA](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2023/06/14/cisa-and-nsa-release-joint-guidance-hardening-baseboard-management-controllers-bmcs)). The guidance asks for hardened credentials, integrity monitoring and regular updates, and network separation of BMC interfaces.

A related client-side example: CVE-2017-5689, a 2017 flaw in Intel AMT (Active Management Technology, a remote management feature) that let an unprivileged network attacker gain system privileges on provisioned machines ([NVD](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2017-5689)).

On Linux, fwupd and the LVFS (Linux Vendor Firmware Service, where vendors publish signed firmware) deliver many of these updates; CERT/CC's PKfail note recommends checking with `fwupdmgr get-updates` and applying vendor updates through the managed update path. Treat firmware like any other patch stream: inventory versions, track advisories, stage rollouts.

blocks.question: A firmware update tool verifies the vendor's signature but accepts any signed version. Which NIST SP 800-147 recommendation does it miss?
options: Secure local update
Rollback prevention: refusing authentic but older images with known weaknesses
Non-bypassability
None
blocks.explain: 800-147 says the authenticated update mechanism should prevent rollback to an earlier authentic version with a known security weakness, for example by comparing version numbers.

blocks.question: Why do CISA and NSA ask for BMC interfaces to sit on a separate management network?
options: BMCs are slow
BMCs cannot use passwords
A BMC can control the server even when it is off and runs below the OS, so exposing it widely gives attackers a powerful, hard-to-see foothold
It improves Secure Boot
blocks.explain: BMCs offer remote control independent of the host OS. Isolating them limits who can reach that control at all, on top of strong credentials and updates.

lessons.title: A defender's firmware playbook, and where to practise

blocks.md:
Plain idea: pull the course into a checklist you can run per device class, and know which signal comes from which layer. Every item below was introduced in an earlier lesson; this lesson is about putting them in order.

**Before you buy or build** (prevention that cannot be added later):

- Hardware root of trust present and *enforcing*: Boot Guard verified mode with the OEM key fused, AMD PSB fused, or Apple's Full Security.
- Firmware sets and locks SPI protections (BLE, SMM_BWP, protected ranges).
- The vendor ships signed firmware updates with anti-rollback, and a recovery path (SP 800-147 and 800-193).
- No test keys: the PK is the vendor's own (PKfail).

**Run and maintain:**

- Secure Boot on, with only the CAs you need in db (on Windows-only machines drop third-party boot loader trust, after checking that no option ROM still needs the Microsoft UEFI CA 2011).
- Track the certificate rollover state per device: 2023 CAs in db and KEK, 2023-signed boot manager, PCA 2011 in dbx, SVN floor; Windows events 1036, 1799, 1037 and 1042.
- Current dbx and SbatLevel; recovery media, PXE images and VM templates rebuilt before each floor is raised.
- Firmware updates applied, including the post-LogoFAIL releases; BMCs updated, isolated and on strong credentials.
- Measured boot with remote attestation where you can: replayed logs, fresh nonces, and alerts on PCR4 and PCR7 changes outside planned rollouts.

**Respond:** a confirmed firmware implant means reflashing or replacing the board, then rebuilding the OS; a confirmed bootkit means rebuilding the ESP and OS and removing any enrolled MOK in person.

scenes.caption: Firmware layer: read-only platform checks (fwupd HSI, CHIPSEC) and scans of the firmware image catch unlocked flash and implants like LoJax.
Secure Boot policy: PCR7 changes, test PKs and missing revocations. Microsoft's events confirm each rollover step.
Boot files: new boot applications appear in PCR4 and in measured boot logs; locked or recently changed files on the ESP point to BlackLotus-style bootkits.
OS side effects: protections switched off and unusual network use are often the first thing anyone sees. Work downward from them.

blocks.md: Each layer can only be checked reliably from the layer below it or from outside the machine. Prefer evidence that a compromised OS cannot forge: TPM quotes, hardware-verified boot, offline firmware dumps compared with vendor images.

**Practise legally.** Run every script in this course yourself; each is standard-library Python and touches nothing on your machine. Extend them: give the toy verifier timestamps, make the event log include a Spec ID header, or make the quote check reject unknown PCR banks. On a Linux machine you own, read (do not change) the platform's posture with `fwupdmgr security`, which prints the HSI results discussed here ([fwupd HSI](https://fwupd.github.io/libfwupdplugin/hsi.html)), and parse a saved event log with `tpm2_eventlog`. Never use flash-writing tools, key-enrolment tools or fuse tools on hardware you cannot afford to lose; fuses are permanent.

For broader systems-security practice: [pwn.college](https://pwn.college/) is a free hands-on platform for core security skills down to assembly and the kernel, and [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/) (the new home of picoCTF) runs capture-the-flag style practice. Test only systems you own or have written permission to test.

blocks.question: A Windows laptop shows a new PCR4 boot application in its measured boot log, PCR7 unchanged, and Defender reported as stopped. Which layer do you examine first?
options: The SPI flash, because PCR7 is unchanged
Only the network
Nothing, PCR7 is fine so Secure Boot passed
The ESP boot files, because a new boot application in PCR4 points to a changed boot chain
blocks.explain: PCR4 records boot applications; a new one means something new ran from the ESP. An unchanged PCR7 only says the Secure Boot variables and the signing authorities used look the same; trusted-but-old binaries, as in BlackLotus, can run without changing them (a new signer, such as the third-party CA behind shim, would show up there).

blocks.question: Which piece of evidence is hardest for malware already running in the OS kernel to forge?
options: A health report from the local EDR agent
A TPM quote over PCRs with the verifier's fresh nonce, checked against a replayed event log
The Windows event log
A screenshot of the setup menu
blocks.explain: The kernel can tamper with agents and logs. It cannot produce a TPM signature over PCR values it cannot reset, bound to a nonce it did not choose.
